title: Global Ice-Cliff Survey Challenges Controversial Accelerated Sea-Level Rise Projections
body:
A team of oceanographers and glaciologists from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOO) has released the most exhaustive field‑based inventory to date of the towering ice cliffs that line the margins of Antarctica and Greenland. The new dataset, gathered over three years of airborne laser scanning, photogrammetry and on‑site measurements, offers fresh insight into a controversial mechanism—known as “marine ice cliff instability” (MICI)—that some climate models invoke to explain rapid, non‑linear sea‑level rise. By quantifying the height, thickness, and structural integrity of thousands of cliffs, the study provides a critical benchmark for testing whether MICI can realistically trigger the dramatic ice loss projected by a subset of future scenarios.

The research team surveyed more than 1,200 ice cliffs across the Amundsen‑Sea sector of West Antarctica, the Antarctic Peninsula, and the north‑western margin of the Greenland Ice Sheet. Using high‑resolution lidar mounted on a Twin Otter aircraft, they captured vertical profiles with centimetre‑scale precision, while unmanned aerial vehicles collected close‑range imagery to resolve surface crevasses and basal melt features. Ground crews drilled boreholes into selected cliffs to measure ice temperature, density, and basal water pressure—key parameters that influence a cliff’s propensity to fail. The resulting catalogue reveals that while some cliffs exceed 200 m in height, the majority are capped at 70–120 m, a range that falls below the critical threshold often assumed in MICI‑driven model runs.

The findings challenge the assumptions embedded in several high‑impact climate projections that predict a sudden, runaway collapse of marine‑terminating glaciers once they retreat past a “critical height” of roughly 100 m. In those models, once a cliff surpasses this limit, it is expected to disintegrate rapidly, unleashing massive ice volumes into the ocean and accelerating sea‑level rise by several meters within a century. However, the WHOO data show that many of the tallest observed cliffs are buttressed by thick, cold ice and exhibit limited basal lubrication, factors that can stabilize them against catastrophic failure. Moreover, the study documents a spectrum of fracture patterns, suggesting that cliff collapse is not a binary event but a gradual process modulated by local geology, ocean temperatures, and seasonal melt cycles.

Critics of the MICI hypothesis have long argued that the theory relies on idealised conditions rarely found in nature. The new observational evidence lends weight to that critique, yet it also underscores the complexity of ice‑ocean interactions. For instance, the researchers identified several “over‑steepened” cliffs that have already begun to slump, shedding icebergs up to 500 m across. These events, while not indicative of wholesale instability, demonstrate that localized failures can still contribute measurable mass loss. The study therefore calls for a nuanced integration of cliff‑scale physics into global ice‑sheet models, moving beyond the simplistic height‑threshold rule toward algorithms that account for material strength, sub‑glacial hydrology, and oceanic forcing.

The broader climate community is taking note. Modelers at leading research centres are already incorporating the WHOO dataset into next‑generation ice‑sheet simulations, aiming to refine predictions of sea‑level rise under various warming pathways. By anchoring theoretical constructs to empirical measurements, the hope is to reduce the wide spread of projected outcomes that currently hampers coastal planning and risk assessment. The study also highlights the importance of sustained field campaigns; without the painstaking aerial and ground‑based work, the debate over MICI would remain largely speculative.

Looking ahead, the authors stress that continued monitoring of ice cliffs is essential as the planet warms. They plan to expand the survey to include the rapidly changing East Antarctic sector and to employ satellite‑based interferometry for near‑real‑time tracking of cliff deformation. As ocean temperatures rise and meltwater penetration intensifies, the balance between stabilising and destabilising forces may shift, potentially bringing some cliffs closer to the critical thresholds once thought unattainable. By establishing a robust observational baseline now, scientists are better equipped to detect early warning signs of accelerated ice loss and to inform policymakers about the realistic range of future sea‑level scenarios.
